name: Guyon canal syndrome (ulnar nerve at wrist)
aliases: ulnar nerve entrapment at the wrist

reference.source: Green's Operative Hand Surgery / Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: Compression of the ulnar nerve within Guyon canal, bounded by the pisiform and hook of hamate and roofed by the volar carpal ligament
The pattern of deficit depends on the zone of compression: zone 1 gives mixed motor and sensory loss, zone 2 pure deep motor branch loss, and zone 3 pure superficial sensory loss
A ganglion arising from the pisotriquetral joint or hook of hamate is the most common cause, followed by hook of hamate fracture and repetitive external pressure
Cyclists develop handlebar palsy from sustained pressure over the hypothenar region
Preserved sensation over the dorsum of the ulnar hand distinguishes this from a cubital tunnel lesion, because the dorsal cutaneous branch leaves the nerve proximal to the canal
Motor involvement produces intrinsic weakness, clawing and a positive Froment sign, with sensory change in the little finger and ulnar half of the ring finger
Wartenberg sign of little-finger abduction may be present with intrinsic weakness
Generic management includes activity modification, padded gloves and wrist splinting, with surgical decompression and excision of any ganglion when a compressive lesion is present
reference.pathophysiology: The ulnar nerve and its branches can be compressed as they traverse Guyon canal at the wrist between the pisiform and the hook of hamate. Common mechanisms include a space-occupying ganglion, fracture or nonunion of the hook of hamate, thrombosis or aneurysm of the adjacent ulnar artery, and repetitive external compression such as prolonged gripping of handlebars. The level within the canal at which compression occurs determines whether the motor branch, sensory branch or both are affected, and dorsal ulnar sensation is spared because its cutaneous branch arises proximal to the canal.
additionalDifferentials: Cubital tunnel syndrome (ulnar nerve at the elbow)
Hypothenar hammer syndrome from ulnar artery injury
A distal ulnar nerve tumour or neurogenic mass
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to localise the lesion to the wrist and distinguish it from an elbow lesion
MRI or ultrasound to detect a ganglion or other soft-tissue mass
Plain radiographs including a carpal tunnel view, with CT when a hook of hamate fracture is suspected
Allen test and vascular imaging when hypothenar hammer syndrome or ulnar artery pathology is considered
Tinel percussion over the canal at the wrist
Assessment of dorsal ulnar sensation to differentiate the level of the lesion
redFlags: Vascular compromise from ulnar artery thrombosis or aneurysm
A mass lesion that may represent a tumour
Nonunion of a hook of hamate fracture as an ongoing source of compression
reference.prognosis: The outlook is good when an identifiable compressive cause such as a ganglion or fracture is treated, though recovery of long-standing intrinsic wasting may be incomplete.
pitfalls: Missing a hook of hamate fracture because standard radiographs are inadequate, requiring special views or CT
Confusing a wrist-level lesion with an elbow-level lesion by not testing dorsal ulnar sensation
Overlooking a vascular cause such as hypothenar hammer syndrome
Incomplete decompression that does not address all involved zones of the canal
